Based on the official Cursor documentation, here's what each tab in the running Cloud Agent view is for. Note that the docs describe these capabilities by feature rather than always naming the exact tab, so I've mapped each tab to the documented functionality.

## Environment
Shows the development environment the agent is running in — the isolated Ubuntu VM with cloned repos, installed dependencies, secrets, startup commands, and network access. From the environment/dashboard view you can see which environment and Build the agent used, environment details, and version history. Configuration (install scripts, `start`/`terminals` commands, Dockerfile, snapshots, secrets, network egress) is defined via `.cursor/environment.json` or the Cloud Agents dashboard, not by editing the VM directly.

## Git
Reflects the agent's source-control work. Cloud agents clone your repo (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket), work on a separate branch, commit, and push changes for handoff — typically as a pull request with demo artifacts attached. This is where you see the diff/branch/PR state of the run. (You need read-write access to the repo and any dependent repos/submodules.)

## Desktop
The agent's remote desktop (its VM's full GUI). Each cloud agent runs with a full desktop environment ("computer use"), so it can drive a mouse/keyboard, open a browser, click through UI flows, and verify changes. **You can take control of this desktop yourself** to interact with the software the agent built — testing GUI apps and flows without checking out the branch locally — then hand control back to the agent so it keeps working.

## Terminal
A view into the agent's VM shell sessions. During agent-led setup you can "watch its progress in a shared terminal session" while it installs dependencies. App-process terminals (from the `terminals` config) run in a `tmux` session **shared by you and the agent**, so this is how you can interactively run commands in the VM alongside the agent.

## Files
A file browser / editor view for the agent's workspace in the VM. The mobile docs explicitly note that the full "Editor, terminal, and file browser" experience "lives on the web" (cursor.com/agents), whereas mobile only shows changed files in a diff view — confirming the web interface provides a workspace file browser for the running agent.

## Subscriptions
Manages what the agent is waiting on so it can keep working without you re-prompting. A cloud agent can subscribe to an event source, end its turn, and wake when a matching event arrives (delivered as follow-ups in the same conversation). Supported sources:
- **GitHub** — PR activity (comments, reviews, lifecycle) and CI results on a branch
- **Slack** — thread replies, channel messages, new public channels
- **Linear** — issue creation/state changes and new comments
- **Timers** — one-off reminders or recurring cron schedules

You create subscriptions by describing the wait in a prompt or via the `/subscribe` skill. They belong to a single conversation and last at most 180 days.

## Can you interactively use the agent's VM?
Yes, in two documented ways:
- **Terminal**: The agent's app-process terminals run in a `tmux` session shared between you and the agent, and agent-led setup exposes a shared terminal session — so you can run commands in the VM.
- **Desktop**: You can take over the agent's remote desktop to interact with GUI apps and the browser, then release control back to the agent.

This works because the cloud agent runs in a fully onboarded remote VM (repo, dependencies, tooling, setup scripts), letting you test changes there without checking out the branch locally. 

One caveat: when the environment is configured purely via a Dockerfile, the docs state "you configure the environment with a Dockerfile; you do not get direct access to the remote machine" for *environment configuration* purposes — but interactive Terminal/Desktop access to a running agent is still a documented capability of the run itself.

A limitation worth noting: the documentation does not explicitly enumerate this exact six-tab layout in one place, so the tab-to-feature mapping above is inferred from the documented Cloud Agent capabilities rather than a single "interface tabs" reference page.
